''den'' = OHG. ''bītan'', MHG. ''bīten'', G. dial. ''beiten'' = Icel. ''bīdha'' = Sw. ''bida'' = Dan. ''bie'' = Goth. ''beidan'', wait. Cf. Ir. ''feithim'', I wait, = Gael. ''feith'', wait. See ''abide''<sup>1</sup> and ''abode''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To remain in expectation; wait.—'''2.''' To be or remain in a place or state; wait.
{{smaller block|In whose cold blood no spark of honour ''bides''.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 1.}}
<poem>Safe in a ditch he ''bides'',
With twenty trenched gashes on his head.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4.}}}}
'''3.''' To dwell; reside.
{{smaller block|<poem>All knees to thee shall bow, of them that ''bide''
In heaven, or earth, or under earth in hell.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 321.}}
<poem>And Lancelot saw that she withheld her wish,
And ''bode'' among them yet a little space
Till he should learn it.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To wait for; await.
{{smaller block|He has the elements of greatness within him, and he patiently ''bides'' his time. {{right|''Prescott.''}}
<poem>I will ''bide'' you at King Tryggve’s hill
Outside the city gates.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' To endure; suffer; bear.
{{smaller block|<poem>Poor naked wretches, wheresoe’er you are,
That ''bide'' the pelting of this pitiless storm.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 4.}}
<poem>Oh, humble me! I cannot ''bide'' the joy
That in my Saviour’s presence ever flows.</poem>
{{right|''Jones Very'', Poems, p. 58.}}}}

'''bidentate''' (bī-den′tāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''biden(t-)s'', having two teeth (see ''bident''), + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Having two teeth or processes like teeth; two-toothed. Other forms are ''bidentated, bidental, bidential,'' and (rarely) ''bidented.''

'''bidential''' (bī-den′shạl), ''a.'' Same as ''bidentate.''

'''bidenticulate''' (bī-den-tik′ū-lāt), ''a.'' [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''denticulate.'' Cf. ''bidentate.''] Having two minute teeth.

'''bidery''' (bid′e̤-ri), ''n.'' See ''bidri.''

'''bidet''' (bi-det′; F. pron. bē-dā′), ''n.'' [< F. ''bidet'' (> prob. It. ''bidetto''), a small horse; of unknown origin.] '''1.''' A small horse; formerly, in the British army, a horse allowed to each trooper or dragoon for carrying his baggage.
{{smaller block|For joy of which I will . . . mount my ''bidet'' in a dance, and curvet upon my curtal.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Chloridia.}}}}
'''2.''' The basin of a water-closet so made that, in addition to the ordinary places of entrance of water- and discharge-pipe, there is a contrivance for washing or administering injections: sometimes made as a separate article of bedroom furniture.

'''bid-hook''' (bid′hu̇k), ''n.'' [A variant of ''beadhook.''] ''Naut.'', a small kind of boat-hook.

'''bidigitate''' (bī-dij′i-tāt), ''a.'' [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''digitate.''] Having two digits, or two finger-like processes.

'''biennial''' (bī-en′i-a̤l), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. Happening or taking place once in two years: as, ''biennial'' games.

Sometimes also ''bisannual''.

'''biennially''' (bī-en′i-al-i), ''adv.'' Once in two years; at the return of two years.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bid|547|bienséance}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|Antagonisms between different powers in the State, or different factions, have caused one or other of them to ''bid'' for popular support, with the result of increasing popular power. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 498.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To bid fair,''' to open or offer a good prospect; seem likely.}}

'''bid''' (bid), ''n.'' An offer of a price; specifically, an offer made or the price offered at an auction: as, to increase another’s ''bid.''

'''bidactyl''' (bī-dak′til), ''a.''   [< L. ''bi-'', two-, + Gr. δάκτυλος, finger, toe.]   Same as ''didactyl.''

'''bidagova''' (bid-a̤-gō′vä̤), ''n.''   [Braz.]   The name given in Brazil to a substitute for coffee prepared from the seeds of the ''Cassia occidentalis. McElrath.''

'''bidale''' (bid′āl), ''n.''   [< ''bid'', invite, + ''ale.'']   An entertainment to which persons were invited for the purpose of contributing to the relief of some one in distress. [Prov. Eng.] Also written ''bidall.''
{{smaller block|There was an antient Custom called a ''Bid-Ale'' or Bidder-Ale, from the Saxon Bidden [''biddan''], to pray or supplicate, when any honest Man decayed in his Estate, was set up again by the liberal Benevolence and Contributions of Friends at a Feast, to which those Friends were bid or invited. It was most used in the West of England, and in some Counties called a Help Ale. {{right|''Brand’s Pop. Antiq.'' (1777), p. 339, note.}}}}

'''bidarkee''' (bi-där′kē), ''n.''   [Also written ''bidarka''; native name.]   A boat of skins used by the Aleutian Islanders.
{{smaller block|There are three miles to traverse to reach the nearest river, and here I trusted myself to one of the far-famed ''bidarkies.'' {{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', XLI. 399.}}}}

'''biddable''' (bid′a̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''bid'' + ''-able.'']   Obedient to a bidding or command; willing to do what is bidden; complying; docile. {{smaller block|She is exceedingly attentive and useful; . . . indeed, I never saw a more ''biddable'' woman.
{{right|''Dickens'', Dombey and Son, viii.}}}}

{{smaller block|A more gentle, ''biddable'' invalid than the poor fellow made can hardly be conceived.
{{right|''H. Kingsley'', Ravenshoe, xliv.}}}}

'''biddance''' (bid′ans), ''n.''   [< ''bid'' + ''-ance''.]   Bidding; invitation. [Rare.]

'''bidder''' (bid′ėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bidder'', ''biddere''; < ''bid'', ask, offer, + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who bids; specifically, (''a'') one who begs; (''b'') one who commands or orders; (''c'') one who asks or invites; (''d'') one who offers to pay a specified price for an article, as at a public auction.

{{smaller block|''Bidders'' at the auction of popularity. {{right|''Burke.''}}}}

'''biddery-ware''' (bid′e-ri-wãr), ''n.'' Same as ''bidri.''

'''bidding''' (bid′ing), ''n.''   [ME. ''bidding'', ''biddinge''; verbal n. of ''bid'' in both the original senses.]   '''1.''' Invitation; command; order; a proclamation or notifying.

{{smaller block|At his second ''bidding'' darkness fled.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 712.}}}}

{{smaller block|They had chalked upon a slate the psalmes that were to be sung, so that all the congregation might see it without the ''bidding'' of a Cleark.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Aug. 19, 1641.}}}}

{{smaller block|Henry . . . nominated Richard Henry Lee and Grayson for the two senators from Virginia, and they were chosen at his ''bidding''.
{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. Const., II. 354.}}}}

'''2.''' The act of making an offer at an auction: as, the ''bidding'' was lively.

'''bidding-prayer''' (bid′ing-prãr), ''n.''   [See below.]   In England, the prayer before the sermon. {{smaller|As directed in the 55th canon of the Church of England, this is a form in which the preacher calls on the congregation to pray for the church catholic, the sovereign, and different estates of men. A similar form of prayer preceding the sermon has been in use since long before the Reformation. At first it was called ''bidding of the beads'' (literally, praying of the prayers), after the Reformation ''bidding of the common prayers'', ''bidding (of) prayers'' or ''prayer'' (the last word being object of the first); but after the sixteenth century the word ''bidding'' came to be popularly regarded as an adjective, or the phrase ''bidding prayer'' as a quasi-compound, a prayer which bids or directs what is to be prayed for. A collect is now generally substituted for the bidding-prayer (and sometimes called by the same name), but on special occasions, and in cathedrals and at university sermons, the bidding-prayer is always used. Liturgiologists often designate the deacon’s litanies of the primitive and the Greek Church as ''bidding-prayers''. See ''ectene'' and ''litany''.}}

{{smaller block|Our people, as of yore, may all join their priest and say along with him, before he begins his sermon, the truly Catholic petitions of the ''bidding-prayer''.
{{right|''Rock'', Church of our Fathers, ii. 354.}}}}

'''biddy'''<sup>1</sup> (bid′i), ''n.''; pl. ''biddies'' (-iz).   [E. dial. and U. S., perhaps of imitative origin. Cf. ''chickabiddy''.]   A familiar name for a hen.

'''Biddy'''<sup>2</sup> (bid′i), ''n.''   [Dim. of ''Bridget'', a fem. proper name, usually given in honor of St. Bridget (Ir. and Gael. ''Brighid'' (gen. ''Brighide'', ''Bride'', whence the form St. ''Bride''), < ''brigh'', strength), who lived in Ireland in the 5th and 6th centuries.]   An Irish female domestic; a servant-girl. [Colloq., U. S.]

'''bide''' (bīd), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bode'', ppr. ''biding''.   [< ME. ''biden'', < AS. ''bīdan'' (pret. ''bād'', pl. ''bidon'', pp. ''biden'') = OS. ''bīdan'' = OFries. ''bīda'' = D. ''beiden'' = OHG. ''bītan'', MHG. ''bīten'', G. dial. ''beiten'' = Icel. ''bīdha'' = Sw. ''bida'' = Dan. ''bie'' = Goth. ''beidan'', wait. Cf. Ir. ''feithim'', I wait, = Gael. ''feith'', wait. See ''abide''<sup>1</sup> and ''abode''.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To remain in expectation; wait.—'''2.''' To be or remain in a place or state; wait.
{{smaller block|In whose cold blood no spark of honour ''bides''.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Safe in a ditch he ''bides'',
With twenty trenched gashes on his head.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4.}}}}
'''3.''' To dwell; reside.
{{smaller block|<poem>All knees to thee shall bow, of them that ''bide''
In heaven, or earth, or under earth in hell.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 321.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And Lancelot saw that she withheld her wish,
And ''bode'' among them yet a little space
Till he should learn it.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To wait for; await.
{{smaller block|He has the elements of greatness within him, and he patiently ''bides'' his time. {{right|''Prescott.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I will ''bide'' you at King Tryggve’s hill
Outside the city gates.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' To endure; suffer; bear.
{{smaller block|<poem>Poor naked wretches, wheresoe’er you are,
That ''bide'' the pelting of this pitiless storm.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh, humble me! I cannot ''bide'' the joy
That in my Saviour’s presence ever flows.</poem>
{{right|''Jones Very'', Poems, p. 58.}}}}

'''Bidens''' (bī′denz), ''n.''   [NL., < L. ''bidens'', having two teeth: see ''bident''.]   '''1.''' A genus of herbaceous composite plants, closely related to ''Dahlia'' and to ''Coreopsis'', having achenes armed with two or more rigid, persistent, retrorsely barbed awns. {{smaller|They are coarse, useless weeds, but some of the species have conspicuous yellow flowers and are known as bur-marigolds. The persistency with which the achenes adhere to clothing and the coats of animals has given rise to the common name of ''beggar’s-ticks'' or ''beggar’s-lice''. The root and seeds of ''B. bipinnata'', known as Spanish needles, have had an ill-founded reputation as emmenagogues and as a remedy for acute bronchial affections.}} '''2.''' In ''zoöl.'', a genus of hawks with two-toothed beak; same as ''Diodon'' or ''Harpagus'' (which see).   ''Spix'', 1834.

'''bident''' (bī′dẹnt), ''n.''   [< L. ''biden(t-)s'', OL. ''duiden(t-)s'', with two teeth, < ''bi-'', ''dui-'', = E. ''twi-'', two-, + ''den(t-)s'' = E. ''tooth''. Cf. ''trident''.]   '''1.''' In ''archæol.'', an instrument or a weapon with two prongs. Hence—'''2.''' Any two-pronged instrument.
{{smaller block|The conversion of the ''bident'' into a trident, by which, instead of two, you chalk three for one.
{{right|''Foote'', in Jon Bee’s Samuel Foote, cv.}}}}

'''bidental''' (bī-den′tạl), ''a.''   [< L. ''biden(t-)s'', with two teeth (see ''bident''), + ''-al''.]   Same as ''bidentate''.

'''bidental''' (bī-den′tạl), ''n.''   [L., so called from the animal sacrificed at its consecration (< ''biden(t-)s'', an animal for sacrifice whose two rows of teeth are complete), or from the forked lightning (a sense of ''bidental'' in ML.), < ''biden(t-)s'', with two teeth or prongs: see ''bident''.]   In ''Rom. antiq.'', a monument marking a place that had been struck by lightning. {{smaller|It consisted of a wall, not roofed, carried around the site, which was considered to be sacred and neither to be trodden nor looked upon, and often resembled a raised well-curb. Such monuments were consecrated by the pontiffs, or, later, by the haruspices, by the sacrifice of a sheep or other victim, and were probably given in charge of guardians, themselves called ''bidentales.''}}

'''bidential''' (bī-den′shạl), ''a.'' Same as ''bidentate.''

'''bidenticulate''' (bī-den-tik′ū-lāt), ''a.''   [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''denticulate.'' Cf. ''bidentate.'']   Having two minute teeth.

'''bidery''' (bid′e̤-ri), ''n.'' See ''bidri.''

'''bidet''' (bi-det′; F. pron. bē-dā′), ''n.''   [< F. ''bidet'' (> prob. It. ''bidetto''), a small horse; of unknown origin.]   '''1.''' A small horse; formerly, in the British army, a horse allowed to each trooper or dragoon for carrying his baggage.
{{smaller block|For joy of which I will . . . mount my ''bidet'' in a dance, and curvet upon my curtal.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Chloridia.}}}}
'''2.''' The basin of a water-closet so made that, in addition to the ordinary places of entrance of water- and discharge-pipe, there is a contrivance for washing or administering injections: sometimes made as a separate article of bedroom furniture.

'''bid-hook''' (bid′hu̇k), ''n.''   [A variant of ''beadhook.'']   ''Naut.'', a small kind of boat-hook.

'''bidigitate''' (bī-dij′i-tāt), ''a.''   [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''digitate.'']   Having two digits, or two finger-like processes.

'''biding''' (bī′ding), ''n.''   [< ME. ''biding'', ''bydyng''; verbal n. of ''bide''.]   '''1.''' An awaiting; expectation. —'''2.''' Residence; habitation.
{{smaller block|At Antwerp has my constant ''biding'' been.

'''bidiri''', ''n.'' See ''bidri''.

'''bidogyn''' (bi-dō′gin), ''n.''   [W., a dagger: see under ''bodkin''.]   In ''Celtic antiq.'', a dagger.

'''bidri, bidry, bidree''' (bid′ri, bid-rē′), ''n.''   [Anglo-Ind., also ''bidery'', ''bidiri'', < Hind. ''bidrī'', < ''Bidar'', a town in the state of Hyderabad, India.]   A kind of ornamental metal-work of India, consisting essentially of damascening of silver upon some metal ground which is made black by coating it with certain chemicals. {{smaller|The alloy used as the basis of the damascene work varies in composition in different localities; it may be either bronze or brass, in the latter case sometimes containing a very large percentage of zinc. Also called ''biddery-ware''.}}

'''bidri-ware, bidri-work''', ''n.'' Same as ''bidri''.

{{smaller block|Why, I tell you, sir: he has been the only ''Bid-stand'' that ever kept Newmarket, Salisbury-plain, Hockley i’ the Hole, Gads-hill, and all the high places of any request.

'''biduous''' (bid′ụ̄-us), ''a.''   [< L. ''biduus'', < ''bi-'', two-, + ''dies'', day.]   Lasting two days only, as some flowers.

'''bieberite''' (bē′bėr-īt), ''n.''   [< ''Bieber'' (see def.) + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.]   Native cobalt sulphate or cobalt vitriol: a decomposition-product of other cobalt minerals found at Bieber, near Frankfort-on-the-Main.

'''bielaga,''' ''n.'' The Russian sturgeon, ''Acipenser huso.''

'''bield''' (bēld), ''n.''   [Now only North. E. and Sc., in Sc. also written ''beild, biel;'' early mod. E. ''bield, beeld,'' etc., < ME. ''beeld, beld, belde,'' < AS. ''byldo'' (= OHG. ''baldi,'' MHG. ''belde'' = Goth. ''balthei''), boldness, courage, < ''beald,'' bold: see ''bold.'']   '''1†.''' Boldness; courage; confidence; feeling of security.—'''2†.''' Resource; help; relief; means of help or relief; support; sustenance.
{{smaller block|<poem>For fuid thou gettis nane uther ''beild,''
But eit the herbis upon the field.</poem>
{{right|''Sir D. Lyndsay,'' The Monarchie, l. 1087.}}}}
'''3.''' Shelter; refuge; protection.
{{smaller block|This bosom soft shall be thy ''beeld.''
{{right|''Fairfax,'' tr. of Tasso, xvi. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|The random ''beild'' o’ clod or stane. {{right|''Burns.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Folk maun bow to the bush that they seek ''beild'' frae.
{{right|''Hogg,'' Brownie, ii. 197.}}}}
'''4.''' A place of shelter.
{{smaller block|These evil showers make the low bush better than no ''beild.'' {{right|''Scott,'' Monastery, I. iii.}}}}

'''bield''' (bēld), ''v.''   [Now only North. E. and Sc., in Sc. also written ''beild, biel,'' etc.; early mod. E. ''bield, beeld,'' etc., < ME. ''beelden, belden,'' < AS. ''bieldan, byldan'' (= OS. ''beldjan'' = OHG. ''baldēn,'' MHG. ''belden'' = Goth. ''balthjan,'' intr.), make bold, < ''beald,'' bold: see ''bold, a.,'' and cf. ''bold, v.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To make bold; give courage or confidence to.—'''2.''' To defend; protect; shelter.
{{smaller block|Scorn not the bush that ''beilds'' you.
{{right|''Scott,'' Monastery, I. xiv.}}}}

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To be bold or confident; grow bold or strong.

''biennium'', a space of two years, < ''biennis'', lasting two years (> ''biennalis'', adj.), < ''bi-'' + ''annus'', year: see ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> and ''annual''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Happening or taking place once in two years: as, ''biennial'' games.
{{smaller block|I consider ''biennial'' elections as a security that the sober second thought of the people shall be law.

'''2.''' Continuing or lasting for two years; changed or renewed every two years: said especially of plants.
